title: Six reasons unwritten papal traditions cannot equal Scripture
pass_a_gloss: First reason: unwritten traditions are deceitful and uncertain in many ways. (1) As to origin: even Peter de Soto admits many things can happen from which it may justly be doubted whether a tradition is apostolic. Modrevius: some theologians of our time by the title of ecclesiastical tradition, if they do not lead us from the Scriptures, yet give traditions first place and Scripture last — what strength can there be in a consensus and in traditions that do not rest on God's Word, and that can be shown not even born from the Apostles if they disagree with and are severed from the divine Scriptures, to which all things must be examined and which must stand firm in God's Church? (2) As to number: at the Ratisbon Colloquy, when ordered to exhibit a certain number of traditions, the papists would not and could not, being doubtful and disagreed among themselves — some refer to tradition heads of doctrine others try to build from the Scriptures. (3) As to discrepancy: some older fathers referred customs of origin not easily shown to the Apostles as if handed down by them, which Chemnitz proves from other ancient writings not to be apostolic. Second: they were proper to Pharisees and heretics (Matt. 15; Mark 7; Irenaeus; Chrysostom; Josephus; Peter de Soto). Third: even if it were most certain some unwritten traditions of Christ or the Apostles remain, equal authority with Scripture could not therefore be given them. Things from the same author have the same authority only when the author freely willed to put that authority in them — not of necessity but of free choice he puts more or less authority in his things, some forever and simply, some for a time and in a certain respect. But God uniquely authorized what He handed down to us in writing through prophets and Apostles, because He handed down Scripture as the perpetual and perfect canon of our life, in which alone is all that is needful for the man of God to be perfect (2 Tim. 3.16). Fourth: those unwritten dogmas that today collide Christians mostly fight openly with Scripture, which all Christians with one mouth confess to be God's Word (Matt. 15; Mark 7; Gal. 1.8; Col. 2.8). Fifth: no adequate cause can be given why things equally needful for those who desire eternal salvation had to be partly written and partly unwritten, since God equally willed the help of Scripture for men's teaching and memory in all things — unless we foolishly say that of things equally needful to salvation some are to be learned and remembered more lightly, others more accurately. Sixth: those very unwritten dogmas, the papists themselves confess, neither were nor could have been kept without the support of some Scripture.
pass_b_english: The first reason is that they are deceitful and uncertain in many ways. First, as to origin. For many things can happen, as Peter de Soto himself teaches in his Defense of the Catholic Confession against Brenz, from which it may justly come into doubt whether some tradition is apostolic. And Andreas Fricius Modrevius: It is no light error of certain theologians of our time who, under the title of ecclesiastical tradition, do not indeed try to lead us away from the Scriptures, yet give first place to traditions and last to Scripture. As if any strength and firmness could be in that consensus and in those traditions that do not rest on the authority of the Word of God — which yet can be shown not even to have been born from the Apostles by this very thing, if they disagree with and are severed from the divine Scriptures, to which all things must be examined, and which must be ratified and firm in the Church of God.

Second, as to number. For in the Ratisbon Colloquy, when ordered to exhibit a certain number of traditions, the papists would not — indeed could not — because they are doubtful of it and do not agree among themselves about it, since some refer to traditions those heads of doctrine which others try to build from the Scriptures. Third, as to discrepancy: because some of the older fathers referred customs whose origin could not easily be shown to the Apostles, as if handed down by them — which yet Chemnitz proves from other writings of the ancients not to be apostolic.

The second reason is that they were proper to the Pharisees and to heretics, as is plain from [[Matthew 15:2 >> Bible:Matthew 15:2]]–7; [[Mark 7:3 >> Bible:Mark 7:3]]–8; Irenaeus Against Heresies 3; Chrysostom on Matthew; Josephus; and Peter de Soto the Dominican in his Defense of the Catholic Confession against Brenz's Prologomena.

The third: because even if it were most certain that some unwritten traditions of Christ or of the Apostles remain, equal authority with Scripture could not therefore be given them. For to things that are from the same author the same authority belongs only when the author put it in and willed it to be in them — who, as an agent acting freely, not of necessity but of free choice, puts more or less authority in his things, and hands some down forever and simply, some for a time and in a certain respect. But God uniquely authorized those things which He handed down to us in writing through the prophets and Apostles, because He handed down Scripture as the perpetual and perfect canon of this our life, in which alone is all that is necessary for the man of God to be perfect ([[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]).

The fourth: because those unwritten dogmas that today set Christians colliding mostly fight openly with Scripture, which all Christians with one mouth confess to be the Word of God — as has been variously and solidly shown by the Protestants, and they are condemned as figments of the human heart ([[Matthew 15:6 >> Bible:Matthew 15:6]]–9; [[Mark 7:7 >> Bible:Mark 7:7]]; [[Galatians 1:8 >> Bible:Galatians 1:8]]; [[Colossians 2:8 >> Bible:Colossians 2:8]]).

The fifth: because no sufficiently fit cause can be given why those things which men desirous of eternal salvation equally ought to know had to be partly written and partly unwritten, since God equally willed the help of Scripture for men's institution and memory in all things — unless perhaps we foolishly affirm that of those things which are equally necessary to salvation some are to be learned and committed to memory more lightly, others more accurately.
The sixth: because those very unwritten dogmas, without the support of some Scripture, neither were kept nor could have been kept, as the papists themselves confess.
source_text: RATIO PRIMA, Quia multis modis sunt fallaces incertae. 1. quod ad originem. Multa enim, ut docet ipse Petrus a Soto in def. cath. conf. contra Brent. cap. 56. contingere possunt, unde merito in dubium veniat, num sit aliqua traditio Apostolica. Et Andreas Friccius Modrevius lib. 4. de Eccles. cap. 7. Non levis, inquit, error est quorundam nostri temporis Theologorum, qui ecclesiasticae traditionis titulo non quidem nos a Scripturis abducere conantur: sed priores tamen partes dant traditionibus, Scripturae posteriores. Quasi vero aliquid roboris ac firmitatis possit esse in eo consensu atque in iis traditionibus, quae non nituntur verbi Dei auctoritate: quas tamen ipsas ab Apostolis minime natas esse, vel hoc ipso argui potest, si discrepent ac disjunctae sint a Scripturis divinis, ad quas omnia examinanda sunt, quaeque in Ecclesia Dei rata esse debent atque firma. 2. Quod ad numerum. Nam in colloquio Ratisponensi sess. 1. p. 24. & 35. Jussi certum traditionum numerum exhibere, id pontificii noluerunt, imo nec potuerunt, quia de eo dubii sunt, neque de eo inter se conveniunt, quia alii ad traditiones ea doctrinae capita referunt, quae alii e Scripturis adstruere conantur. 3. quod ad discrepantiam: quia nonnulli patres vetustiores consuetudines, quarum origo non facile demonstrari poterat, ad apostolos, quasi ab ipsis traditas, retulerunt, quas tamen Apostolicas non esse, ex aliis veterum scriptis probatur a Chemnitio part. 1. Exam. C. T. de trad. p. 146. seqq. SECUNDA est, quia Pharisaeorum & haereticorum propria fuerunt, ut liquet e Matth. 15.2.3.4.5.6.7. Marc. 7.3.4.5.8. & Irenaeo lib. 3. adversus haereses cap. 2. pag. 250. Joh. Chrysostomo tom. 2. homil. in Matth. col. 435.436. Josepho, Petro a Soto Dominicano in def. cath. conf. adv. proleg. Brentii cap. 56. TERTIA, Quia, si maxime constaret traditiones quasdam non-scriptas a Christo vel ab Apostolis superesse, non tamen propterea par illis authoritas cum Scriptura tribui posset. Nam iis, quae ab eodem authore sunt, tum demum eadem constat authoritas, cum eandem indidit & inesse voluit author, qui, tanquam agens libere, non ἐξ ἀνάγκης ex necessitate, sed ἐκ προαιρέσεως ex praeelectione libera plus minusve authoritatis rebus suis indit, & quaedam in perpetuum & simpliciter, quaedam ad tempus & secundum quid tradit. Jam vero Deus, quae scripta nobis tradidit per prophetas & Apostolos, ea singulari modo authoravit, quia Scripturam, ut hujus vitae nostrae perpetuum ac perfectum canonem tradidit, in quo solo omne id est, quod necessarium est, ut homo Dei sit perfectus, 2. Tim. 3.v.16. QUARTA, Quia dogmata illa non-scripta, quae hodie collidunt Christianos, pleraque manifeste pugnant cum Scriptura, quam Dei verbum esse Christiani omnes uno ore confitentur, ut a Protestantibus varie, solideque demonstratum est, & tanquam cordis humani figmenta damnantur, Matth. 15.6.7.8.9. Marc. 7.7. Gal. 1.8. Col. 2.8. QUINTA, Quia nulla satis idonea causa afferri potest, cur ea, quae homines aeternae salutis cupidos aeque scire oportuit, partim scribi, partim non scribi debuerint, cum Deus hominum institutioni & memoriae aeque in omnibus Scripturae adminiculo consultum voluerit: nisi forte stulte affirmemus, ex iis, quae ad salutem aeque sunt necessaria, alia levius, alia accuratius perdiscenda, memoriaeque mandanda esse. SEXTA, Quia illa ipsa non-scripta dogmata absque Scripturae alicujus praesidio nec servata fuisse, nec servari potuisse, ipsi Pontificii fatentur.
